## What the scanner says about that asset

`crimes scan --format json` returns one finding for it — `crime_00038`, charge **"Icon-Sized Raster"** (`raster_should_be_vector`, pack `universal`), on `src/assets/check-icon.png`:

> **summary:** "32×32 PNG icon-sized raster. SVG would scale cleanly across DPIs and ship smaller; the current asset locks the image to a single resolution."

Evidence, verbatim:

> - `"dimensions: 32 × 32 px (≤ 64 threshold both sides)"`
> - `"format: png"`
> - `"consider replacing with an SVG icon — same render at every DPI, smaller bytes"`

Scored `severity: low` / `confidence: 0.85`, `effort: "quick"`, `fix_shape: "ship the SVG source; rasters lose at any scale"`, with the suggested action `switch_to_svg_icon`.

## Why a new SVG indicator beats another PNG at those dimensions

**32 × 32 px is the entire asset.** That's 1,024 pixels of information and no more. Every render path that isn't exactly 32 CSS px on a 1× display is resampling: a 2× display draws it at 64 device pixels and a 3× phone at 96, so the check mark softens on precisely the screens your users are most likely to be looking at. The finding's phrasing is the point — the asset "locks the image to a single resolution." The usual workaround is shipping `@2x`/`@3x` siblings, which turns one indicator into three files that must stay visually in sync forever.

**The threshold is the tell.** `≤ 64 threshold both sides` is the detector's way of saying this is icon geometry, not photographic content. Icons at this size are flat shapes — a tick, a dot, a ring — which is exactly the class of image vector describes losslessly and in fewer bytes than a bitmap of the same shape.

**A status indicator has more states than a check mark does.** This is the strongest argument specific to your case. A status indicator generally needs several colors (pending / ok / warning / error), plus a dark-mode variant. In SVG that's one file whose `fill` is `currentColor`, recolored from CSS. In PNG it's one file per state × per DPI — a four-state indicator at 1×/2×/3× is twelve assets, and the scanner will eventually flag those too.

**Copying the pattern propagates a flagged one.** `check-icon.png` isn't a neutral precedent to imitate; it's already an open finding. A second PNG at these dimensions adds a second `raster_should_be_vector` finding rather than reusing something the repo has blessed.

## One caveat before you export

"Make it an SVG" is not automatically the fix. The same scan carries `crime_00034` — **"SVG With Embedded Raster"** on `src/assets/partner-logo.svg`, at `severity: high` / `confidence: 0.95`, with evidence `"2 \`<image href=\"data:image/…;base64,…\">\` occurrences"` and `"SVG byte size: 592 bytes (includes the base64 overhead)"`. Its summary is blunt about the failure mode: *"The SVG mime type promises infinite scale, but the actual pixels are locked to one resolution — usually larger than a plain PNG."*

That finding is rated **higher severity than the PNG it would be replacing**. So if your export path is "open the PNG in a design tool, save as SVG," you'll trade a low-severity finding for a high-severity one. The new indicator needs to be real vector geometry — `<path>`, `<circle>`, `<rect>` — authored from the vector source (Figma/Sketch/Illustrator), as `crime_00038`'s suggested action notes: *"If the source is a designer's PNG, the original vector likely exists in Figma / Sketch / Illustrator — re-export from there."*
